The spread of NAD(P)-binding across several SCOPe folds implies that nucleotide-cofactor binding has been acquired more than once, and that it is a functional constraint which many different protein architectures can satisfy. It does not by itself show that those architectures share an ancestor. Two cases matter. First, within the Rossmann-like class c.2 (NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains, superfamily c.2.1), many enzymes (short-chain dehydrogenases, lactate/malate-type dehydrogenases, GAPDH-like enzymes and others) share a beta-alpha-beta core and a glycine-rich turn (GxGxxG-type) that packs the pyrophosphate at the N-terminus of a helix. This is good evidence for common ancestry at the superfamily level, but the motif itself is short and recurrent. Second, FAD/NAD(P)-binding enzymes in class c.3 (FAD/NAD(P)-binding domain, superfamily c.3.1) bind the dinucleotide with a different topology, and some medium-chain zinc alcohol dehydrogenases use a separate non-Rossmann NAD-binding domain. Taken together, the data fit a model in which at least some nucleotide-binding solutions arose independently (convergent), while the Rossmann-type solution is best explained by divergence within a superfamily. Multi-fold distribution alone cannot settle which case applies to a given enzyme.

Cofactor binding or active-site similarity alone is insufficient for homology because: (1) NAD(P) binding is a recurrent functional requirement, so shared cofactor binding is expected under convergence; (2) short motifs such as GxGxxG or catalytic His/Asp/Ser/Tyr residues recur by chance and are not diagnostic in short alignments; (3) active-site geometry and chemistry (hydride transfer, proton shuttling) can be reproduced by unrelated scaffolds, and catalytic residues are often recruited into new folds; (4) a ligand-contact template from a different fold confers no evolutionary relationship. The SCOPe criteria are therefore hierarchical: fold membership denotes a common major architecture (which may or may not reflect homology), superfamily membership is the level at which common ancestry is usually inferred from structural core, mechanism and, where possible, phylogenetic signal, and family membership requires clear sequence or structure similarity. A cofactor-binding site may appear at any of these levels.

Required external evidence before inferring homology or transferring function between NAD(P)-binding proteins includes: a structural superposition of the conserved core (not only the cofactor site), sequence profile or HMM evidence beyond the binding motif, phylogenetic analysis showing that the proteins share a common ancestor rather than convergent clustering, and biochemical or kinetic evidence for the claimed function (cofactor specificity, mechanism) in the query protein. Limits: I used pretrained knowledge only, so I could not verify exact SCOPe release identifiers or current domain assignments offline; the fold and superfamily assignments above are stated at the level I am confident in, and specific domain IDs should be checked against the SCOPe release. Representative selection should avoid mixing folds, and annotations should not be transferred across fold boundaries on the basis of cofactor binding alone.
